extracted.intended_audience: agency officials and administrative law practitioners (attorneys, agency staff), interested members of the public
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for agency notice-and-comment rulemaking, publication of rules/opinions, access to records, hearings, and related adjudicative procedures under an Administrative Procedure Act–style statute. Covers when notice/procedure are required, exceptions, and evidentiary/hearing standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of organization, business places, methods, and substantive rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Every agency is required to publish in the Federal Register its (1) organization, (2) places of doing business with the public, (3) methods of rule making and adjudication including the rules of practice relating thereto, and (4) such substantive rules as it may frame for the guidance of the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication must be kept up to date. Enumerated classes of informational rules must be separately stated (e.g., procedure separate from substance). Agencies must also publish internal delegations of authority. The subsection forbids secrecy of rules binding or applicable to the public and protects the public from being required to resort to unpublished organization or procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited exceptions to publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Introductory clause states only general exceptions — matters requiring secrecy in the public interest and matters relating solely to internal agency management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions are necessary but not to be construed to defeat the purpose of the remaining provisions. Examples include confidential investigative or prosecuting aspects of Secret Service or FBI. Internal management exceptions may not permit withholding of operations that other provisions require to be public. Exceptions apply only 'to the extent' that the excepted subjects are directly involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication or availability of final opinions and orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are required to publish or, pursuant to rule, make available to public inspection all final opinions or orders in the adjudication of cases except those held confidential for good cause and not cited as precedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should formulate and publish a rule respecting access to final opinions/orders so the public knows how to secure such information. 'Rulings' (general interpretations) if authoritative would be covered by substantive rule category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of public records
rubrics_metrics.description: Except as statutes may require otherwise or information may be held confidential for good cause, matters of official record are to be made available to persons properly and directly concerned in accordance with rules to be issued by the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should classify data to specify what may be disclosed and must provide how and where applications for information may be made, how they will be determined, and who will do so. Refusals of information are subject to requirements of section 6(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking exceptions (military/foreign/management/proprietary etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4 exempts from its requirements rule making so far as there are involved (1) military, naval, or foreign affairs functions or (2) matters relating to agency management or personnel or to public property, loans, grants, benefits, or contracts (and proprietary matters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exceptions do not relieve agencies from other statutory requirements. 'Foreign affairs functions' is to be narrowly interpreted (only those affecting international relations). Proprietary exception intends to facilitate issuance of rules by dispensing with mandatory procedure. Exceptions do not encourage agencies to avoid voluntary public procedures and apply only to the extent the subject is directly involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice content for proposed rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: General notice of proposed rule making must be published in the Federal Register and must include (1) time, place, and nature of proceedings, (2) reference to authority under which held, and (3) terms, substance, or issues involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice must fairly apprise interested parties so they may present responsive data/argument. The subsection does not apply to rules other than those of substance or where agency for good cause finds notice and publication impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest (and publishes the finding and reasons). Definitions/explanations of 'impracticable', 'unnecessary', and 'public interest' are provided to limit abuse of exemptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity to participate and statement of basis and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: After notice, the agency must afford interested persons an opportunity to participate in the rule making at least to the extent of submitting written data, views, or argument; and, after consideration, the agency must incorporate in any rules adopted a concise general statement of their basis and purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets the minimum required public procedures short of statutory hearing; agencies may also hold informal hearings, consult advisory committees, etc. Agencies must analyze and consider all relevant matter presented and explain the actual basis and objectives of the rule with reasonable fullness. Where other statutes require hearings, those requirements control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deferred effective dates for substantive rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The required publication or service of any substantive rule must be made not less than 30 days prior to its effective date except (1) as otherwise provided by the agency for good cause found and published or (2) in the case of rules recognizing exemption or relieving restriction, interpretative rules, and statements of policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 30-day deferred effective date is not necessarily a maximum; agencies may require longer periods. 'Good cause' exceptions require legitimate grounds supported in law and fact. Where authority beneficial to the public does not become operative until a rule is issued, agencies may issue immediately and rely on later public reconsideration to satisfy requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to petition for issuance/amendment/repeal of rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Every agency is required to accord any interested person the right to petition for the issuance, amendment, or repeal of a rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions apply to effective rules and to proposed/tentative rules; agencies should receive petitions for modification of published proposed rules. Upon petition, agency must fully and promptly consider the request, take action as required, and pursuant to section 6(d) notify the petitioner if denied. The agency may grant, initiate public rulemaking, or deny; mere filing does not require grant or hearing. Denial is not per se subject to judicial reversal, but facts may require agency action to avoid judicial vulnerability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and applicability of adjudication provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions relating to adjudications apply only where the case is otherwise required by statute to be determined upon an agency hearing, except certain classes of operations are expressly not affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated exceptions include (1) cases subject to trial de novo in court, (2) selection or tenure of public officers other than examiners, (3) decisions resting on inspections, tests, or elections, (4) military, naval, and foreign affairs functions, (5) cases in which an agency is acting for a court, and (6) certification of employee representatives. Exceptions apply only to the extent the subject is directly involved. Sections 2,3,6,9,10,12 still apply where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice requirements for agency hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons entitled to notice of an agency hearing are to be duly and timely informed of (1) the time, place, and nature of the hearing, (2) the legal authority and jurisdiction under which it is to be held, and (3) the matters of fact and law asserted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where private persons are moving parties, respondents must give prompt notice of issues they controvert. Agencies must give due regard to convenience and necessity of parties when fixing times/places, and must ensure the affected party has ample notice and time to prepare. The purpose is to simplify issues for benefit of parties and deciding authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity for settlement or adjustment before hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must first afford parties an opportunity for the settlement or adjustment of issues (where time, nature of proceeding, and public interest permit), followed, if issues are not settled, by hearing and decision under sections 7 and 8.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary settlement-by-consent provision is important and limited to cases where time, nature, and public interest permit; it does not give agencies arbitrary discretion. Examples when exception applies: lack of time, extremely numerous parties, or immediate administrative execution needed to protect public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of investigative/prosecutorial and adjudicative functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers who preside at the taking of evidence must make the decision or recommended decision in the case and may not consult with any person or party except openly and upon notice; prosecuting officers may not participate in decisions except as witness or counsel in public proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents investigating/prosecuting officers from influencing or controlling hearing/deciding officers except in public proceedings; ex parte matters (adjournments, filings) are excluded. Exemptions include initial license applications and 'past reasonableness of rates' cases and top agency members, but agencies should not apply exceptions where fair procedure is required (e.g., accusatory cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to issue declaratory orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Every agency is authorized in its sound discretion to issue declaratory orders with the same effect as other orders, limited by the introductory clauses of section 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declaratory orders may be issued only where agency is empowered by statute to hold hearings and the subject is not expressly exempted. Agencies are not required to issue declaratory orders merely because requested; 'sound discretion' precludes improvident orders and issuance is governed by principles like those for declaratory judgments in courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of appearance and counsel before agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person compelled to appear in person before any agency or its representative is entitled to counsel. In other cases, every party may appear in person or by counsel. Interested persons may appear before responsible officers at any time for presentation or adjustment of any matter, so far as responsible conduct of public business permits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies are to proceed with reasonable dispatch to conclude matters presented, with due regard to convenience and necessity of parties. 'Party' means a person showing requisite interest. The subsection does not take a position on nonlawyers representing parties; agencies retain the right to regulate admission of nonlawyers. Agencies should not impose burdensome bar admission requirements on lawyers in good standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on investigative process and access to copies
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative process is not to be issued or enforced except as authorized by law. Persons compelled to submit data or evidence are entitled to retain or, on payment of costs, to procure copies; in nonpublic proceedings a witness may for good cause be limited to inspection of the official transcript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provision is designed to preclude 'fishing expeditions' and investigations beyond agency jurisdiction. In grand-jury-like nonpublic proceedings, limiting copies may be necessary to protect prosecutions; nevertheless parties should have copies or inspection opportunities to assure evidence is correctly set forth and for legal/administrative uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for issuance and contest of subpoenas
rubrics_metrics.description: Where agencies are by law authorized to issue subpoenas, parties may secure them upon request and upon a statement or showing of general relevance and reasonable scope if the agency rules so require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a party contests a subpoena, the court should inquire generally into the situation and, if the subpoena is in accordance with law, order production under penalty of contempt. This assures private parties the same access to subpoenas as agency representatives and prevents improvident or overly burdensome subpoenas. Courts should not engage in detailed examination of matters committed to agency authority but should be satisfied that agency could possibly find it has jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt notice and statement of grounds for denials
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompt notice is to be given of denials of requests in any agency proceeding, accompanied by a simple statement of grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement of actual grounds should apprise the party of basis for denial and any other administrative remedies. A statement need not be made when affirming a prior denial or where denial is self-explanatory, but prior grounds must remain the actual grounds and be sufficient to notify the party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality and disqualification of presiding officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearings must be held by the agency, its members, examiners, or other authorized officers; all presiding and deciding officers are to operate impartially and may withdraw if they deem themselves disqualified. Upon filing of a proper affidavit of personal bias or disqualification against them, the agency is required to determine the matter as a part of the record and decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presiding officers must ensure hearings are conducted impartially while maintaining order and adduction of necessary evidence. Agency determinations on affidavits of bias become part of the record and are subject to administrative and judicial review. Discovery of bias late may render decisions invalid, so care is required to avoid sitting where disqualified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers of presiding officers at hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Presiding officers, subject to agency rules and within its powers, have authority to (1) administer oaths, (2) issue such subpoenas as authorized by law, (3) receive evidence and rule upon offers of proof, (4) take depositions or cause depositions to be taken, (5) regulate the hearing, (6) hold conferences for settlement/simplification of issues, (7) dispose of procedural requests, (8) make decisions or recommended decisions under section 8, and (9) exercise other authority as provided by agency rule consistent with the bill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This list does not expand agency powers but assures the presiding officer performs a real adjudicative function rather than merely a notary or policeman. The agency should not conduct hearings 'from behind the scenes' where it cannot know detailed happenings in the hearing room.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standards and burden of proof in hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Except as statutes otherwise provide, the proponent of a rule or order has the burden of proof. Any evidence may be received, but agencies are required to exclude irrelevant and unduly repetitious evidence and no sanction may be imposed or rule or order be issued except as supported by relevant, reliable, and probative evidence. Parties may present oral or documentary evidence, rebuttal evidence, and conduct reasonable cross-examination. For rule making or initial license applications, agencies may adopt procedures for submission of evidence in written form so long as parties are not prejudiced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative hearings are compared with equity proceedings; mere admission of evidence is not reversible error, but findings must rest on evidence that is material and competent. Agencies may not arbitrarily disbelieve credible evidence; applicants need not be presumed unlawful without requisite proof. Cross-examination rights extend to written evidence submitted under permissible procedures. Agencies should apply standards of probity and reliability analogous to courts, excluding irrelevant or unduly repetitious evidence as a matter of good practice.
